title: OpenAI’s math solutions aren’t meeting the field’s standards yet
key_facts: TechCrunch says OpenAI released hundreds of claimed solutions to hard maths problems this week after saying it had consulted an advisory group, and fell short of the group's standards.
The group, AGMAI, hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, has nine prominent researchers and issued guidelines at the end of September.
Its first request was to stop testing advanced maths problems on proprietary models; OpenAI's release says it is doing exactly that.
OpenAI followed some principles, such as releasing quickly and including information on how the model reached results, but only 10 of the 719 manuscripts included the model's chain of thought.
A new paper from Cambridge and King's College London documents at least two discrepancies between the written and Lean versions of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes proof.
Harvard's Melanie Wood told TechCrunch there is no human understanding of such results at release, "and now the work begins".
AGMAI did not respond to TechCrunch's request for a fuller evaluation.
quote_evidence: But OpenAI fell short of those standards, particularly where the mathematicians emphasized the need for human understanding of a mathematical result.
But not for all of them: Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model’s chain of thought.
why_it_matters_hint: OpenAI said it would follow a panel's guidance on AI maths results and, on TechCrunch's reading, did so only in part.
notes: TechCrunch's sentence on the share of proofs without formalisation (42%) conflicts with Yellow.com (about 42% formalised) so it is not used. Judgment of "falling short" is TechCrunch's. Same cluster as C04-01, C04-06, C04-07.
